title: Five of five new players quit at my AI story game's character question, so I stopped asking
author: Business-Pension-498
selftext:
I make Selkie, interactive novels an AI writes around your choices. Last week I looked at where new players stopped. From 13 to 18 November, every one who reached the "Who are you?" question left there: five of five. None of them typed a word or tapped one of the three ready-made characters I'd added to make it easier. It wasn't a bug. A character sheet before the story starts is homework, given before anyone has a reason to care.

So now you start as the story's own lead. The question moved into the menu as "Make them yours", for whenever you like. The hard parts were all about changing a character mid-story:

* **Renaming the past.** The new name has to replace the old one in pages already written, in recaps, summaries, memories and the notes each character keeps. Titles have to survive: "Dr. Kowalczyk" becomes "Dr. Novak", not "Novak Kowalczyk".
* **Keeping what the story did.** Stats are rebuilt for the new character, then everything the story has moved since the start goes back on top. Relationships stay as they are.
* **Nobody notices.** For the next two passages the narrator is told this person has always been who the reader says. Where an earlier page differs, the new description wins.
* **Undo.** Rewind would have brought the old character back, so keeping a new one clears it.

Talking it over with the character builder costs no turns. It's capped at five changes a story, with one nudge on chapter 1's closing page.

Too early to know if it works: nobody new has joined since it went live. How do you handle character creation in LLM games? Up front, later, or never?

[https://playselkie.com/?from=reddit-aigamedev2](https://playselkie.com/?from=reddit-aigamedev2)

comments.author: dr0idattack137
comments.body: I read this as “just get players into the game”, right? Good insight that I might apply to my game

replies.author: Business-Pension-498
replies.body: Yes, pretty much. Ask players anything before they've seen the game, and you lose some of them. I moved my question into the menu, with one reminder at the end of chapter 1. Hope it helps with yours.

comments.author: Xinnobun
comments.body:
People are probably leaving because they assume (not necessarily correctly) that there's not much substance to the game if AI is essentially weaving the story for them. After all, they could achieve something similar by using their own LLM.  
Plus there are hundreds of these already from other websites.

They are looking for something that stands out from the crowd, does yours?

replies.author: Business-Pension-498
replies.body:
Fair question. I think you're right that people assume it's a thin wrapper. Most of the hundreds you mean are chats with one character. This is closer to a novel with game rules. A form in front of the first page didn't help: it asked for work before showing any of that.

What a chat with your own LLM doesn't give you:

**1. Dice it can't fudge.** Risky moves show their odds, then code rolls. A model left to itself tends to let you win. Here a failed roll stays failed, and the next passage has to deal with it.

**2. A plot you can't see.** Each story is planned before you start: chapters, a hidden plot, several endings. The narrator writes toward them. You find them by playing.

**3. Memory kept in code.** The calendar, who knows what, how each person feels about you. A few characters also act on their own between your turns. Before you read a passage, a second pass checks it against what has already happened.

Whether that stands out enough is what I'm trying to find out. Now it has to show on the first page, with nothing in front of it.

replies.author: Xinnobun
replies.body:
You also can't ask too many or too personal questions. Because then it crosses a line of data collections for players, and thats a red flag for many. 

I noticed your game is from a website. How much does it cost to host it?

replies.author: Business-Pension-498
replies.body:
Agreed. Selkie asks for an email or a Google sign-in, so your story is saved. It also asks your age, since most stories are 18+. Anything about your character is optional and belongs to that story, not to your account.

Hosting is cheap. The server is one small always-on machine, about $6 a month. The database, sign-in emails and the website run on free tiers for now. The real cost is the AI: about 12 cents a turn on the cheapest narrator, more on the others. So it's sold by the turn, as ink.

comments.author: ScrywareDev
comments.body: Five for five quitting at the same screen is brutal, but at least it told you exactly where the problem was. I have had the same thing with first screens. The player has not bought into anything yet, so any friction at all and they are gone. Have you had any new players through since you moved it to the menu? That is the part I always struggle with, getting fresh eyes on the fix instead of the same testers who already know where everything is.

replies.author: Business-Pension-498
replies.body:
Only two so far, so it's too early to call. One reached page 4, further than anyone got last week. The other signed in and never opened a story, which is a different leak.

I have the same problem with fresh eyes. I know where everything is, so my own playing tells me nothing about the opening. What helps is counting. Each post gets a link with its own tag, so I can see how far the players from it got. Every post is a small test of the opening, this one included.
